sentences.text: The genus is known from a single partial vertebra that possesses unusual features not found in other sauropods. The centrum of the preserved vertebra is estimated to be 200 mm long, with a preserved height of 300 mm. The posterior face of the centrum has an average diameter of 165 mm and features a concave surface.

The neural arch leans forward at an angle of 35 degrees and has broad areas of featureless bone on its lateral surfaces. The neural canal is large and teardrop-shaped at the front but small and circular at the back opening.
The bone remained largely unnoticed for 113 years while stored at the British Natural History Museum in London.
Estimates suggest the type individual was between 15 and 20 meters long and weighed between 2.8 and 7.6 tonnes, depending on its body proportions.
Fossil collector Philip James Rufford discovered the vertebra in the early 1890s. The fossil was found near Hastings in East Sussex, England, within the Hastings Bed Group.
The specimen was briefly described by Richard Lydekker in 1893. The new genus was officially announced by the British Palaeontological Association on November 15, 2007.
Xenoposeidon was a large quadrupedal herbivore, similar to other sauropods.
Xenoposeidon is classified within the class Saurischia.
Researchers initially classified Xenoposeidon as a neosauropod of uncertain affinities because it did not fit comfortably into established groups.
Xenoposeidon belongs to the parent group Rebbachisauridae. The family of Xenoposeidon is Rebbachisauridae.
A 2018 study by Taylor reclassified Xenoposeidon as a basal member of Rebbachisauridae, placing it 10 million years older than Histriasaurus.
Xenoposeidon lived during the Berriasian to Valanginian stages, between 139.1 and 132.6 million years ago.
Some phylogenetic analyses have classified Xenoposeidon as a nomen dubium because the fossil material is considered nondiagnostic.
